title: Nurse-led weight clinic versus usual advice for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis in first-opinion practice
subtitle: Pragmatic trial across 12 companion animal practices
statement: Overweight dogs with osteoarthritis are common in the group's practices, but vet-led advice rarely produces sustained weight loss. A nurse-led weight clinic run in two practices is popular, and the board is considering rolling it out. A pragmatic trial in everyday practice will compare the clinic with usual advice on owner-reported mobility at six months, with weight, blinded lameness assessment, pain relief use and retention as secondary outcomes.
whoAffected: Overweight dogs with osteoarthritis and their owners; registered veterinary nurses who would run the clinics; vets; and the practice group deciding whether to fund roll-out.
whatHurts: Excess weight worsens joint pain and mobility, owners watch their dogs slow down, and pain relief is prescribed without addressing a modifiable cause. A roll-out that does not work would take nurse time from other care.
currentPractice: Weight advice and a diet leaflet during the consultation, pain relief as needed, and few follow-up weight checks.
whyNow: The board is deciding on roll-out, two practices have a year of clinic experience, and ethics approval and nurse time are in place.
constraints: No external funding; the practice group covers nurse time and a discounted therapeutic diet. Enrolment must fit normal consultation times, and each practice can run at most two weight clinic sessions a week. Dogs in the usual-care group cannot be asked to attend extra visits beyond a six-month review.
patientCenteredGoal: Overweight dogs with osteoarthritis move more comfortably, as their owners judge it, with no loss of welfare from hunger or reduced pain relief.
summary: Problem framed as a pragmatic effectiveness question comparing a nurse-led weight clinic with usual advice.
